label: paragraph_title
text: MOST ESSENTIAL.

label: text
text: There are services and services that must be maintained during the strike. Some are of lesser importance than others. One of the most essential is undoubtedly the sanitary service. At all costs that must be kept going to the utmost capacity. At all costs—let that be repeated! There must be no possible risk of an epidemic of disease following the epidemic of idleness. In normal times the Sanitary Department is badly understaffed. One inspector for an area the size of a fairly large village at Home cannot be said to be enough for local conditions. It is streets—if not miles—off the ideal. What can be said of that staff during a period of emergency such as the Colony is passing through at present? And there is the army of sanitary coolies. They stood by the Department during the 1922 strike. On the present occasion intimidators have got to work—and the rest has been easy. Still, not all the Sanitary coolies are out and it is essential that these should be paid a wage commensurate with the vital importance of their work—the most necessary of any work in the Colony. It is believed that there is a sufficiency of coolie labour at the prevailing market price. That is an important factor in relation to the health of the Colony. But it is as well to publish the assurance for the benefit of the public in general—non-Chinese and Chinese.

label: text
text: God bless Esperantists! They at any rate are trying to subdue the spoken word of all nations to one uniform level, so that man

label: text
text: may understand man. Perhaps the greatest disaster that ever befell sinful man was that unhappy incident of the Tower of Babel, when tongues— at one time of equal sense—became confused. From that time dates conflicts, strifes, misunderstandings and all the rest of human waywardness. Is not a universal language the panacea for most of the ills of life? True, people of the same tongue quarrel, and, misunderstand, but the means are quickly at hand to readjust and make plain. Not so with those who speak in divers tongues. The civilised mind cannot, for instance, quite grasp the fact that those of the same race fight each other to the death. This civil strife in China—to the foreigner at any rate—is inexplicable. He asks questions and is given the reason. China is a land of many languages and dialects. One district cannot understand another. To those of one Province, the members of another are foreigners, if necessary to be treated in the most arbitrary fashion. This explains why Yunnanese are prepared to fight Cantonese, and contrariwise. Each to the other is a foreigner—an enemy, a suspect. And so it goes on. From which it would appear that nothing permanent in the peace line will occur until the babel of tongues in China is brought down to one common factor. It is a big job—but no bigger than following a campaign of slaughter. And the results will unquestionably be more lasting.

label: paragraph_title
text: AN APPEAL.

label: paragraph_title
text: CORRESPONDENCE.

label: paragraph_title
text: STRIKE PAY.

label: text
text: (To the Editor of the China Mail).

label: text
text:
Sir,—When I read in your columns that part of the resolution passed by the Kowloon Residents' Association in regard to payment of wages for the days in June during which the servants had worked, I rubbed my eyes and read it again to make sure that my eyes had not played me false. Yes, there, it was as plain as can be "such payment to be spread over a probationary period of at least one week." Ye gods! We know well that the boys are not justly entitled to any wages at all—having broken their contract—and we sternly say "No Boy!! I cannot pay you your wages to day, you have forfeited them by striking, but I will pay you in seven days' time."
PRAYER FOR THOSE IN CHINA.

label: text
text:
The K.R.A., I presume, are acting upon the Hongkong Chamber of Commerce's recent recommendation. It might be as well therefore if they were to get in touch with that body when they would, I think, be informed that the probationary period the Chamber had in mind was from six to eight months! So that the final payment might fall somewhere about China New Year. What on earth is the use of one week? You might just as well pay the boys on the day of their return for all the told over than that such a course would give you.
"YOURS are"
"TIME OF CRISIS."

label: paragraph_title
text: U. S. AND CHINA.

label: text
text: London, July 6.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The United States' "well-meaning suggestion" to reform immediately extra-territorial rights in China is the theme of a long leader in the Daily Telegraph which declares that by doing so at the present hazardous moment the United States would be assuredly regarded by Japan as having at last thrown down the gauntlet.

label: text
text: The paper points out that of all the Foreign residents with interests in China the Japanese would not only suffer most by a modification of extra-territorial rights but in the present—mood—of—the Chinese, the Japanese would be so patently menaced that, pacific as its present intentions are, Tokyo would be persuaded by the mere instinct of self-preservation to take immediate action.

label: text
text: The editorial adds that side by side with the anti-foreign movement, the next few months will see the development in Manchuria of a fierce triangular struggle between Chang Tso-lin, Japan, and Red Russia. Unless Chang, with or without outside assistance, is able to enforce a definite limit to the continual penetration of Russia "the Island Kingdom must intervene."

label: text
text: The paper ends by slying that if to this necessity is added an attempt by the United States to weaken the guarantees which Japan now enjoys in China, there can be only one end to the affair.

label: paragraph_title
text: MILL FRACAS.

label: text
text: Shanghai, July 6.

label: text
text: On Saturday night, a Municipal constable arrested a Chinese who had been firing crackers in the street. He detained the prisoner in a cotton-mill compound pending the arrival of the police car.

label: paragraph_title
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: Hundreds of Chinese gathered in front of the mill, where they were addressed by two agitators, who urged them to attack the mill. The constable arrested one of the agitators, who struggled and attempted to seize the constable's revolver.

label: text
text: Other Chinese rushed up, while the cotton mill employees went to the constable's assistance.

label: text
text: An American seaman, named Dizik, belonging to the U.S.S. McLeish came on the scene and, seeing that the situation was critical, fired, shooting through the head of a Chinese who was about to jump upon the constable from behind. The crowd then dispersed.

label: text
text: The two agitators were arrested and will appear in the Mixed Court to-day.

label: text
text: The wounded Chinese died last night. Two foreign onlookers from the mill state that the American's action averted a serious situation.

label: paragraph_title
text: DANCERS KILLED.

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: Boston, July 5.

label: text
text: While a hundred persons, were participating in the Fourth of July celebrations at the Pickwick Club early in the morning and an orchestra was playing dance music, a wall of a five-storey building, weakened by adjacent excavations, crashed down on the dance floor, entrapping the dancers between the floor and the fallen metal ceiling work.

label: text
text: Rescue was most difficult, necessitating the removal of the front wall which threatened to collapse in addition to the debris. Hitherto twelve dead were brought out after a night and daylong search. Voices, chiefly of women, were heard calling for help from the debris early in the morning but became silent later.

label: paragraph_title
text: FALSE REPORTS.

label: text
text: (Router's Service.)

label: text
text: Hankow, July 5

label: text
text: The American Chamber of Commerce has written to the Chinese Chamber of Commerce to endeavour to make known to the Chinese the true facts of the Hankow affair.

label: text
text: After warning the Chinese Chamber of the danger of allowing false reports—the American note says that there is nothing to add to the despatches from the Consuls to the Chinese authorities on June 15, which contained a complete and irrefutable statement on the Hankow incident, and encloses copies.

label: text
text: Attention is drawn to efforts being made to throw the full responsibility for the incident on the British authorities and the note says: it so happened that a point in the British Concession was attacked, but as the British Naval officer in charge of that post acted for the International community of Hankow, we, as part of the combined defence force which included French, Italians, Japanese and Americans, as well as British, must therefore accept our share of the responsibility of their action.

label: text
text: "We stand by them wholeheartedly, and urge you in fairness to co-operate in making this fact clear to the Chinese people."

label: paragraph_title
text: HENLEY REGATTA.

label: paragraph_title
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: Dull weather prevailed at Henley to-day, but a large 'crowd witnessed the finals in the various events. In the final for the Visitors' Cup, Third Trinity College (Cambridge) beat Brasenose (Oxford) by two lengths in 7 minutes 45 seconds. In the Grand Challenge Cup, Leander beat the Thames Rowing Club by three quarters of a length in 6 minutes 53 seconds, which is a record for the course.

label: text
text: In the Diamond Sculls, Beresford beat Gollan easily in 8 minutes 28 seconds.

label: text
text: Beresford interviewed after the racing said that he had relinquished the Philadelphia Gold Cup which he had handed back to the American oarsman Hoover.

label: text
text: His ground for doing this was that the English Amateur Rowing Association insisted that the Diamond Sculls constituted the World's Amateur Championship, and not the Philadelphia Cup as claimed by the Americans.

label: text
text: In the Stewards' Cup, Third Trinity (Cambridge) beat Leander by 2 lengths in 7 minutes 27 seconds.

label: text
text: In the Ladies' Lady Margaret, (Cambridge), beat Radley College by 2 lengths in 7 minutes; 7 seconds.

label: text
text: In the Wyfold Cup, the Thames Rowing Club beat Selwyn College (Cambridge) by $1\frac{1}{4}$ lengths in 7 minutes 35 seconds.

label: text
text: In the Thames Cup, First Trinity (Cambridge) beat the Henley Rowing Club by 1 length in 7 minutes 16 seconds, and in the Silver Goblets, Third Trinity (Cambridge) beat Leander by 4 lengths in 8 minutes 17 seconds.

label: text
text: (Router's Service.)

label: text
text: Paria, July 6.

label: text
text: A message from Fez states that violent Riff attacks were made on the night of July 5 on a group of French positions at Upper Leben, near Ainnatouf, and were repulsed with heavy losses. The French advanced north-west of Kiffane after a sharp engagement in which arms and munitions were captured. In view of the recent enemy infiltrations, women and children have, as a precaution, left Taza.

label: paragraph_title
text: DOSSER'S TRIAL.

label: text
text: The evidence in the Dosser case was continued this morning. Two Russians, Detective Bebenim and Constable Kedrolizansky, who accompanied a British detective to arrest the accused couple, described the finding of incriminating documents, with especial regard "to a certificate from the Soviet Agitation Department.

label: text
text: Cross-examined, Bebenim admitted that he once worked for the Bolsheviks at Vladivostock, but denied that when sent on a Soviet mission from Vladivostock, he embezzled Soviet funds. He, however, admitted being sent on such a mission.

label: text
text: Kedrolizansky admitted that before joining the Municipal Police in Shanghai he was an officer in the White Russian Army at Vladivostok, also that he was formerly a political enemy of the Bolsheviks, who imprisoned him at Vladivostok. He was only released when the Japanese took over the port.

label: text
text: The case was adjourned until to-morrow.

label: paragraph_title
text: EUROPEAN CHARGED.

label: text
text: ALLEGED BREACH OF TRUST.

label: text
text: In the District Court at Singapore a European, named Mr. W. W. Matthews, was charged with criminal breach of trust in respect of $2,000 worth of watches belonging to Messrs. V. R. Vick and Co. Chief Court Inspector Meredith asked for a postponement for further investigations, as the accused was only just arrested.

label: text
text: The accused, who pleaded, not guilty, objected to a postponement, stating that if there was a case against him it was a civil case. He added that he was not an agent, but a partner with Mr. Vick, and that about $4,000 must be due to him from Mr. Vick.

label: text
text: Mr. Franklyn Robinson adjourned the case for a week, fixing bail at $2,000.

label: text
text: Shanghai, July 5.—Mr. MacMurray, the newly-appointed U.S. Minister to China, left Shanghai this afternoon on an American gunboat. He is expected to arrive in Tientain to-morrow afternoon. Reuter.

label: text
text: Washington. July 6.—Reports hitherto received by the War Department indicate that the test muster for defence forces yesterday was only two thirds as great as in September. Nevertheless the results are considered satisfactory.—Reuter's American Service.

label: text
text: Paris, July 8.—That protracted Franco-German commercial negotiations have broken down is attributed to the fact that both countries are about to introduce new Protectionist tariffs and that it is impossible to conclude a permanent convention until these are passed by Parliament.—Reuter.
